pairs.subject: imported-material-conformance
pairs.evidence: src/__tests__/lib/visual-gen/material-boundary-swatch.test.ts:88 The swatch that checks all three outputs together (preview, Blender, UE) covers base colour on both sides of the sRGB curve but holds roughness at the 0.5 midpoint and metallic at 0. Separate per-output tests each check one off-centre gloss value (Blender 0.25, UE 0.2 with metallic 1, preview 0.7), but no shared known object spans both gloss extremes and no per-role ramp is read back.

techniques.evidence: src/components/modules/visual-gen/material-lab/MaterialPreview.tsx:22 The preview takes each map's colour space from the single per-role table in material-boundary.ts. The Blender script and the UE material-instance script read the same table; the UE script also sets each texture's sRGB flag and refuses one asset wired into roles of opposite colour space.

src/__tests__/lib/visual-gen/material-boundary-swatch.test.ts:88 The swatch puts base colour on both sides of the curve but leaves gloss at the midpoint (the inversion's fixed point). No metallic pair at both extremes runs across the outputs. Per-role colour space is checked by counting flag strings, not by pushing a stepped ramp through.

src/components/modules/visual-gen/material-lab/materialPreviewProps.ts:59 Every participant uses the roughness convention: three.js MeshStandardMaterial, Blender's Principled Roughness and UE's Roughness scalar. Each map stays separate, so nothing needs negating or moving to another channel.

src/components/modules/visual-gen/material-lab/useMaterialStore.ts:145 The lab is the in-project author and always states every parameter it sends. No outside delivery reaches it with omitted properties, which is this technique's 'when not to use' case.
